title: Artificial intelligence: Council gives final green light to simplify and streamline rules
date_evidence: On 29 June, the Council of the EU has given its final green light to the AI Act simplification package, following the European Parliament's formal endorsement on 16 June 2026 ... the new application dates would be 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk AI systems and 2 August 2028 for high-risk AI systems embedded in products.
key_claim: The Council gave final approval to the AI Act simplification package (part of Omnibus VII) on 29 June 2026, following the European Parliament's endorsement on 16 June 2026; the application of high-risk AI obligations is deferred to 2 December 2027 for stand-alone high-risk systems and 2 August 2028 for high-risk AI embedded in products, and national AI regulatory sandboxes are postponed to 2 August 2027.
frame_summary: The Council presents the AI Act rollback as pragmatic simplification that preserves protection while giving providers and authorities more time, framing deferral as good regulatory housekeeping rather than retreat.
notes: Consilium press page is JavaScript-rendered and returns an empty body to plain fetches; date and content captured from WebSearch snippets per the date-capture protocol step 4(a) and corroborated by mirrored coverage (EEAS delegation reprint, Agence Europe, DLA Piper and White & Case client alerts).

title: Novelle des Produkthaftungsrechts unterschiedlich bewertet (public hearing on the Product Liability Modernisation Act, Drucksache 21/4297)
key_claim: At the Bundestag legal affairs committee's public hearing on 13 April 2026, experts assessed Germany's transposition bill divergently: the government bill undertakes the first comprehensive reform of German product liability law since 1989 and brings software, including AI systems, into strict product liability regardless of how it is provided or used; the DIHK criticised the draft for extending the scope beyond what EU law requires, Professor Schmidt-Kessel identified 'fundamental expansions of liability' at a whole series of points, and the German Bar Association criticised new presumption rules on defect, causation and damage as strongly changing civil law.
frame_summary: Germany's parliament records a contested transposition: the government frames the bill as overdue modernisation extending strict liability to software and AI, while industry and parts of the legal profession argue it expands liability further than the directive demands and injects uncertainty through new presumption rules.
notes: German-language Tier 1 source satisfying the multi-language sourcing protocol; hearing content summarised by Bundestag press service.

title: The right balance: how to fix European Union artificial intelligence regulation (Policy Brief 12/2026)
date_evidence: Publishing date 11 June 2026 ... Mariniello, M. (2026) 'The right balance: how to fix European Union artificial intelligence regulation', Policy Brief 12/2026, Bruegel
key_claim: Bruegel recommends that EU AI regulation trade lower ex-ante burden for robust ex-post monitoring, judicial review and liability: recalibrate the AI Act's ex-ante requirements by expected deployment scale, introduce an AI ad-hoc ex-post liability system with effective ex-post monitoring and supervision, and increase ex-post transparency; it identifies the absence of an AI ad-hoc liability mechanism as a gap and argues high expected costs such as fines and liability indemnities force developers to internalise the consequences of failing to minimise harm.
frame_summary: Bruegel argues the EU should deliberately rebalance AI governance away from ex-ante compliance towards ex-post liability and supervision, treating credible litigation exposure as the efficient substitute for the paperwork the simplification agenda is cutting.
notes: Institutional think-tank design argument that makes the ex-post shift a recommended architecture rather than an accident of politics.

title: EU Product Liability Directive: Responding to Software, AI and Complex Supply Chains (client alert)
key_claim: Directive (EU) 2024/2853 applies to products placed on the EU market after 9 December 2026 and expands strict liability to stand-alone software, digital manufacturing files and integrated digital elements; it introduces disclosure obligations for litigants, rebuttable presumptions of defectiveness and causation (including where claimants face excessive difficulties due to technical or scientific complexity, particularly relevant for black-box AI), new liability for online platforms, an expanded circle of liable operators including importers and fulfilment providers, compensation for psychological harm and destruction of personal data, and eliminates the previous EUR 500 property-damage threshold and liability caps; as of the alert only Germany and the Netherlands had published legislative transposition proposals.
frame_summary: Gibson Dunn advises that the directive imports discovery-style disclosure and claimant-friendly presumptions into all EU member states, making documentation, supply-chain mapping and contractual risk allocation the decisive defensive assets for software and AI businesses.
notes: Structural anchor (3-6 month band): the canonical practitioner analysis of the directive's mechanics used for the structural framing; the directive text itself (November 2024) sits outside the permissible window.

title: EU Product Liability Directive Tracker 2026
key_claim: Across the CEE/SEE region most member states have not yet transposed the new PLD and several remain in the pre-implementation phase with no draft legislation published (Austria, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria as at March 2026); Hungary has already transposed the directive; Croatia ran a public consultation on its draft in February-March 2026; Slovakia's draft was expected to reach government in May 2026; Bulgaria's implementing act is expected to be finalised by August 2026 and approved by parliament in November 2026.
frame_summary: The firm's tracker frames transposition as a live patchwork: a handful of front-runners against a majority of member states still drafting, with litigation-risk implications varying country by country as the December 2026 deadline approaches.
notes: Regional law-firm tracker; primary evidence base for the transposition-lag strand and for the counter-argument.

title: EU Product Liability Directive Creates New AI and Software Liability Risks
key_claim: Under the revised regime products may become defective if necessary software updates or security patches are not provided; courts may obtain broader powers to require disclosure of technical documentation, source code, training records and technical logs during litigation; industry stakeholders have raised concerns that broader liability exposure could increase litigation activity and insurance costs across software-reliant sectors; the practical scope of provisions on disclosure, software defects and complex AI systems will be shaped through litigation across member-state courts and potentially the CJEU.
frame_summary: The legal trade press argues the directive converts software lifecycle management, cybersecurity and AI governance into a single litigation-exposure surface, with documentation becoming a core component of legal risk management rather than a regulatory formality.
notes: Quality specialist trade press; corroborates the disclosure and update-liability strands.

title: Representative Actions Directive (policy page)
date_evidence: Evergreen Commission policy page, no publication date; page states the Directive 'entered into application at national level' on 25 June 2023 and that 'up to date not all EU Member States have transposed the Directive'.
key_claim: The Representative Actions Directive (EU) 2020/1828 requires every member state to provide a mechanism for representative actions by qualified entities seeking injunctive and redress measures on behalf of groups of consumers, across areas including data protection and financial services; member states may choose opt-in, opt-out or combined mechanisms and may permit third-party litigation funding subject to conflict-of-interest safeguards.
frame_summary: The Commission presents collective redress as functioning EU-wide access-to-justice infrastructure with deterrent effect on rogue traders, balanced by safeguards against abusive litigation.
notes: Evergreen reference for the collective-redress infrastructure strand; accessed 06/07/2026.
